<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

# Types of Terrain Tiles

<a href="#types-of-terrain-tiles"
id="user-content-types-of-terrain-tiles" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: Types of Terrain Tiles"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

Mapzen Terrain Tiles provide worldwide basemap coverage sourced from
[SRTM](/tilezen/joerd/blob/master/docs/www.openstreetmap.org) and other
open data projects with several different data formats and varying
levels of processing.

The following formats are available, with full details below:

- `terrarium` with extension `png` in Web Mercator projection, 256x256,
  260x260, 512x512, and 516x516 tiles
- `normal` with extension `png` in Web Mercator projection, 256x256,
  260x260, 512x512, and 516x516 tiles
- `geotiff` with extension `tif` in Web Mercator projection, 512x512
  tiles
- `skadi` with extension `hgt` in unprojected latlng, 1°x1° tiles

Need help displaying raster tiles in a map? We have several
[examples](/tilezen/joerd/blob/master/docs/build-a-map.md) using Mapzen
raster tiles to style in your favorite graphics library including
Tangram.

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## Terrarium

<a href="#terrarium" id="user-content-terrarium" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: Terrarium"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

**Terrarium** format *PNG* tiles contain raw elevation data in meters,
in Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857). All values are positive with a
32,768 offset, split into the red, green, and blue channels, with 16
bits of integer and 8 bits of fraction.

In other words, the red channel encodes the "256s" place, the green
channel the "1s" place, and the blue channel the fractional component,
which is 0 - 0.99609375 (255/256) in increments of 0.00390625 (1 / 256).

To decode:

`(red * 256 + green + blue / 256) - 32768`

To encode, asuming a starting value of `v`:

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="v += 32768
r = floor(v/256)
g = floor(v % 256)
b = floor((v - floor(v)) * 256)">

``` notranslate
v += 32768
r = floor(v/256)
g = floor(v % 256)
b = floor((v - floor(v)) * 256)
```

</div>

For example, with a starting value of 2523.266:

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="v += 32768
&gt; 35291.266
r = floor(v/256)
&gt; 137
g = floor(v % 256)
&gt; 219
b = floor((v - floor(v)) * 256)
&gt; 68

&gt; rgb(137, 219, 68)">

``` notranslate
v += 32768
> 35291.266
r = floor(v/256)
> 137
g = floor(v % 256)
> 219
b = floor((v - floor(v)) * 256)
> 68

> rgb(137, 219, 68)
```

</div>

Decoded, this gives us:

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="(r * 256 + g + b / 256) - 32768
&gt; 2523.265625">

``` notranslate
(r * 256 + g + b / 256) - 32768
> 2523.265625
```

</div>

The range of the elevation data (-11000 - 8900 meters) spans
`rgb(85, 8, 0)` - `rgb(162, 198, 0)`, or
`[0.33203125, 0.03125, 0] - [0.6328125, 0.7734375, 0]`.

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## Normal

<a href="#normal" id="user-content-normal" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: Normal"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

**Normal** format *PNG* tiles are processed elevation data with the the
red, green, and blue values corresponding to the direction the pixel
“surface” is facing (its XYZ vector), in Web Mercator projection
(EPSG:3857). The alpha channel contains **quantized elevation data**
with values suitable for common hypsometric tint ranges.

- `red` = x vector
- `green` = y vector
- `blue` = z vector
- `alpha` = quantized elevation data

High alpha channel values indicate lower elevation values (below sea
level), making them more opaque. Specifically, **normal** format alpha
values are counted in (floored) elevation increments. Below sea level
they start at -11,000 meters (Mariana Trench) and range to -1,000 meters
in 1,000 meter increments, with more detail on the coastal shelf at
-100, -50, -20, -10 and -1 meters and finally 0 (intertidal zone).
Values above sea level are reported in 20 meter increments to 3,000
meters, then 50 meter increments until 6,000 meters, and then 100 meter
increments until 8,900 meters (Mount Everest).

Encoding quantized height ranges
([src](https://github.com/tilezen/joerd/blob/master/joerd/output/normal.py#L26-L41)):

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="for i in range(0, 11):
    table.append(-11000 + i * 1000)
table.append(-100)
table.append( -50)
table.append( -20)
table.append( -10)
table.append(  -1)
for i in range(0, 150):
    table.append(20 * i)
for i in range(0, 60):
    table.append(3000 + 50 * i)
for i in range(0, 29):
    table.append(6000 + 100 * i)">

``` notranslate
for i in range(0, 11):
    table.append(-11000 + i * 1000)
table.append(-100)
table.append( -50)
table.append( -20)
table.append( -10)
table.append(  -1)
for i in range(0, 150):
    table.append(20 * i)
for i in range(0, 60):
    table.append(3000 + 50 * i)
for i in range(0, 29):
    table.append(6000 + 100 * i)
```

</div>

To decode quantized height value:

`255 - bisect.bisect_left(HEIGHT_TABLE, h)`

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## GeoTIFF

<a href="#geotiff" id="user-content-geotiff" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: GeoTIFF"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

**GeoTIFF** format tiles are raw elevation data suitable for analytical
use and are optimized to reduce transfer costs in 512x512 tile sizes but
with internal 256x256 image pyramiding, in Web Mercator projection
(EPSG:3857). See
<a href="http://www.gdal.org/frmt_gtiff.html" rel="nofollow">GDAL
documentation</a> for more information.

Allow for the larger tile size by referring to the tile coordinate of
{z-1} parent tile.

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## Skadi

<a href="#skadi" id="user-content-skadi" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: Skadi"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

**Skadi** format tiles are raw elevation data in unprojected WGS84
(EPSG:4326) 1°x1° tiles, used by the Mapzen Elevation lookup service.
Essentially they are the SRTMGL1 format tiles but with global coverage
and compressed using gzip. See
<a href="http://www.gdal.org/frmt_various.html#SRTMHGT"
rel="nofollow">GDAL documentation</a> for more information.

See the <a
href="https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/sites/default/files/public/measures/docs/NASA_SRTM_V3.pdf"
rel="nofollow">SRTM</a> guide for exact format specifications, which are
summarized below:

- The DEM is provided as 16-bit signed integer data in a simple binary
  raster. There are no header or trailer bytes embedded in the file. The
  data are stored in row major order (all the data for row 1, followed
  by all the data for row 2, and so on).

- Tiles are compressed in a gzip format and have a '.hgt.gz' type
  extension.

- All elevations are in meters referenced to the WGS84/EGM96 geoid as
  documented by the <a
  href="http://earth-info.nga.mil/GandG/wgs84/gravitymod/egm96/egm96.html"
  rel="nofollow">National Geospatial Agency</a>.

- Byte order is <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endianness"
  rel="nofollow">Motorola ("big-endian") standard</a> with the most
  significant byte first. Since they are signed integers elevations can
  range from -32767 to 32767 meters, encompassing the range of elevation
  to be found on the Earth.

- These data also contain occasional voids from a number of causes such
  as shadowing, phase unwrapping anomalies, or other radar-specific
  causes. Voids are flagged with the value -32768.

</div>
